div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
(By Redcap.)
THE TURKEY

.... What glorti us weather we're having ! The eurkoo has emu,, the young grass is sbootirg forth and its grand weather for young turkeys! It is never wise to hatch turkeys too early in the season, they really e inrot stand cold winds sail wet weather during t!e first pencil of their PXlBlellee. Therefore, yin may proceed to hatch turkey eggs now with some degree of safety. •
KEEI.I,_ AND REOIN,

..... .............. . To keep and rear turkeys successfully the locality stout be suitable. A free range over fields which are well wooded is the very best of all localities. Turkeys should never be roosted in elm d houses, open sheds or even in the branches of trees is far ben, than keeping thrm too confined. When they have full liberty and esrecially if the fields are wooded with oak, beech, and chestnut) they find most of their own (wt. The natural food which falls from these trees in autumn, is notch relished by the young stock. The nearer you rear torkeys under natural conditions, so much finer is the flavour of the flesh. Where it is not possible to allow a free range, Bed when it is the desire to raise a few turkeys, then the utmost atten- tion should be paid toabsolutecleanliness, and perfect ventilation r f rdeeping qusrters.

The turkey-hen site for a period of lrom thirty to I thirty-one days. As she generally lays about twenty eggs before becoming broody, a portion should he put under common hens the same day as the turkey begins incubation. Twelve to fifteen eggs are as many as at will well rover: of course the whole of the broods could be given to the turkey when hatched out, site will by nature give better attention than a common hen. Turkey chicks are very tender and delicate at first, therefore it is lit tor that they remain unmolest,if with the turkey lien for a fow days ; at the same time it in eosential that you make an early examination of the chicks and attend to insect I yes at once. After the second or third day providing the weather is fine and warm, the hen may be cooped Dittos graos. Provide a good layer of fine jeat moss on the II or of the c. op. Nothing is more detrimental to young turkeys than dampness. The first few meals for the chicke should consist of liard-builed eggs chopped fine and mixed with bread crumbs and groat.. Green food, chopped very fine, roust lie added, of which dandelion, chickweed, lettuce and young onions are among the very best. What,ver kind of wat •r vessel you may use, tee that the chicks do not get into it; let it be very shallow, for on it matter of fact, if a young turkey chick gets thoroughly wet it nearly always proven fatal. The food r .onmended for the chickens mny be continued until they ate ate ns mough to digest foods more in accordance it ills natural condi- tions, such as soft grain and y,ung natural herbage. As the reason advances Jut them have sevens to the harvest fields where they will continue to thrive ott what they pick up in a natural way.

The chicken stage is mostly about two or three months. 'Hien the nipples on the head a, d neck begin to swell and change in colour to very bright red. lMting this period it is tl.e moat critical time of all ill the life of a turkey. Consequently they need plenty of invigorating food. At this stage afore- mentioned they emerge into turkey pouts and with prone: care and attention they nil! get through this trying period ; after which they are little trouble to manage.
I,I7TENING

When the turkey poults have reached the age of about five 'months. yon should feed them more liberally on wholesome food-stufis so as to assist them in putting on flesh more rapidly. It is always better to separate the aexen for they tilt ive and fatten quicker sun result. Ito not allow them to roans too much during the process of fattening. The following may be given for the first few weeks every morning: Boiled r ,takes mashed and mixed INA pea-meal, biscuit-meal, main lineal and barley. This mash should be given at least twice a day, being careful to remove any that ia left over. Let all feeding and drinking utensils he kept acruntilously clean. As an alternative and a mange you may give them a grain feed of good wheat and oats.
I,NEIt Al. lIESI %It A,.

Witten there are not the conveniences for rearing, it is a groil plan to purchase a few voting poults and fatten them off. Ala-a3s be careful and patellaae them after the " almoting of the red " as previously poihted out, this is surmised to be the langer point in the bfe of a turkey. It is always better to purchase females, as they fatten much quicker and I think the flesh a the turkey hen is more delicate than than of the" nobblcra." A large open-fronted shed oith a good floor covering of leaves and straw litter makes an ideal fattening place for tinker. Keep them clean and feed on good wholesome food .d a ready market will await your labours for good specimens.

The To douse and the White Etribden geese are the most potular as well as the most useful varietiest to keep. If you have a small pond aid a gcs I grass i run t is racy to rear (very profitably) a good batch of geese. Providir g that you take vile of the youngsters for the first two or three weeks they will with little attention take care or themselves. Now is the time to set the eggs for Christmas markets. At this season of the year there is a big demand for home products, and I often w. ncler how it is that our British farmers allow so much foreign competition with the popular Christmas Goose." There is not much difficulty in raising quite a good number from one pen of adults and even if you have to purchase eggs or young geslings it certainly pays and pays well. They nr,d very little attention and they need also very scanty housing accommodation. Still further if a fl k of young geese are allowed the fete range over a meadow they do it an incalculable amount of good. They will rid old pasture land of weed and at the same time fertilise the land. Tire period of incubation for gooBo3 egg, is from 2.4 to 34) days. Common hens may be utilised profitably for hatzbing purposes, lad don't be tempted to risk too many eggs with one hen, four or five are ample according to the size of /leo used. The goslings should be fed an pr young turkeys for the first few days, after which the following makes a good food.

Boiled potatoes, biscuit tneal, and third:u. Pont overfeed them until they are full grown then you may gives more substantial diet so as to enable them to to Tut on flesh.

div.p: ATHLETICS
Local Track Needed.

To-day Hallatnahire abould have visited Warrington Athlstic Club for inter club contest at one mile (220, 220, 110, 0801 two miles (8•11, 1)40, 8110, 840 the( wiles team race Owe to run, three to count) and the members of the local club had been looking forward to handicaps at 103, 200, 600 and 1,200 yards on the flat, one mile cycle •nd novelty race, but being unable to obtain • suitable ground and track, local enthusiasts will have to wait for the sport, and local tradespeople will be v ithout the business these inter club contest. would Lave brought to the town. That • local cyclist must travel nearly 20 miles for a training spin on • respectable track, that the majority of local athletics roust train ea opportunity • tiers in the lanes and byc • v ays does not tend to develop their abilities- indeed the wonder is that they do on well under such condi- tions—it is, therefore, high time that something wee done to provide training facilities under which quantity and quality may Improve, otherwise the colt 01st hletics must wane and jeoperdire local promotions. Can the local club relict the support of sportsmen ? The isilure to bring off to-cley's fixture bag proved a grevous disappointment, to allay which handicaps at :100 and I,COO yards will be run, on the 27th inst., also a , cycle race if sufficient interest can be aroused. Theae I events are intended to be self-supporting if possible. .0 .11 concerned ahould immediately communicate with the hon. sec., Mr. C. [terry, who will doubtless provide all information concerning the handicaps also the annual social and prime distribution which takes place I in the sante date.

LIBERAL WOMEN AND SUFFR.ACIE. The Women's Liberal Federation meeting at Mao. cheater on Tuesday decided to urge the selection of Liberal candidate. favourable to Woman Suffrage and to work only for candidates pledging thensselyeg to support any Suffrsge Bill against which the Liberal Whips do not tell. Lady Bamford Slack proposed a resolution congratulating the Government on the satis- factory pro eeeee ti de with the Parliament 11111, and commented on the quack remedies offered to the Mouse of Lords by Lansdowne for the long-standing disease of arrogance.

Cricket Notes. Saturday was a great day forfoiloweracf the glr rious summer spott fo-. with ideal weather prevailing, practically all the !coal clubs were engaged and some capital sport was witnessed. The Warrington eleven had ample canine for satisfac in in the victcry which marked the opening match f the teas. at Arp'ey. Ashton-under-Lyne were the visitors and although the home club had not a strong side doicg duty, the bowling end fielding of the Warringtonians was en keen that their opponents were handsomely accounted for. That fine young cricketer T. Wright vas a notable absentee fr,ma the home ranks He has for the time being thrown in in lot with Larlestown, L r whom he km clad up ,67 again,t St. Helens Recs. on Saturday. Batting first no a a-,merrhat slow wicket, lVarrington opened in disccuraging fashion, two wickets being down for fire tans —thanks to the puzzling deliveries of Lambe. re.,tell, the new pro- fessional, and S. Bartr:due put a rosior complexion on the g one, the '' pro " innrkirrg an invaluable 18 before he wan caught behind the wick. t by Butler, whilst the amateur made a sound 12. B. Silcock, the home skipper, was even more su,cessfel in imploring Warrington's prospects, for he hit out frealy arid elm- piled 19. The innings closed for SI, Lambe having reined the fine howling analysis of C wickets for 11

If omens count for much, Pea'sli cert. iris made a very suspicions beginning as a bowler on tie Atpley pit,b, the first ball be sent down being so tamely received he the Ashton captain that the professional had no difiicul y inbringing di • catch. The War- rington bowlers made no mistake and the fielding was :leo particularly smart. The visitors collapsed ignominiously, the only batsman to cfrer anything like a serious tesistance being It. Kershaw. who was di,- missed for 11. Partridge gave a grand bowling display and came out with the unique analysis of three wickets for no runs. Pesten was also in capital form and captured three wickets for 19 runs, while Bennett did well in taking four for 19.

Warrington 2nd met sterner foes at Ashton-under- lone where the La! smen had a much better chance than at Warrington. The •isitors saved the match by a good margin. Ashton running up the substantial score of 171 to which Warrington had responded with ' 112 for 8 wickets when lime was called. in the silt- ing side the great featnre was the Itri.li at batting of A. T. L. Greer who carried out his bat with the substantial score of 32. W. V. Turton also showed excellent form for his 22 and J. Hawthorn contributed a useful 16. For Ashton A. Yosall tl2 not out). J. Humphreys (36) and J. Bray (37) were chiefly prominent.

The Warrington and District League has again got into full swing and five matches were derided on Satmday. Under their rem name ,f Warriogtm Conservatives, the champions made a promising start by trouncing Sankey to the tune of 113, J. Constable distinnuishing himself with a brilliant inning. fix 47-13 more than the combined efforts of the Sankey men realm. 1. Green Ids, did yeoman service with the bat.
There was a close encounter between Ryiands Bros. and Orford, the villegPrs being victorious by 4 runs. It Rai a match of small srores, G. Gough (18) haying tie hint figorno to his credit.

Whi!ecioss have got a good team together this season, but they had their work cut cut to account for such doughty opponents ea Sankey Wire Mills. How- ever, they st..cceeded in doing it, but ohly three runs separated the teams. The individual efforts were on the whole of a mediocre description, Lot W. Bernett gave a good display for his 19. Latchford Wesleyana administered a terrific drubbing to Wilderspo,l Brewety, tanning them all out for 22 and responding with the nice round total of 115. Ashton deserves special praise for a smart not out inning. of IG, while other batsmen, who achieved notable things were J. Knight (.13) and Toulmin (29). Shakeshaft and Ashton wrought great (lance with the ball.

There were also some interesting friendly matches. Stockton Heath Juniors were victorious at the expense of Workingmen'. Mission who, howeA er, put up a plucky fight, and had to admit defeat t i the extent of nit-ti rut.. J. Ma:Artily (17) was the on'y player to obtain double figura..
8.,1d-stleet Junior Wesleyans did badly against Holy Trinity, who placed 52 to their account and dismksed the Wealeyans for iS. Ilainsworth (12) and Lfealey (12 not nut) wele the top scorers.

Carter heading the scores with an • xcellent t'.2. Widnes were in indifferent form and were all out for 413, the best indiv:dual score berg 11. Ice's 10.

The visiting bowlers bad a merry time, the only [lrina batsmen who gave any trouble being H.Shorrocks and S. H. Parker (15 each) end 11. Wilke (11.) For Ashley F. Hill batted in fine style, his score realizing 31 without disturbance of his w.ckets.

The Lancashire County Individual Merit Competi- tion, which is a very popular feature in bowling, will be more no this year owing to the committee's decision to play this gigantic competition in sections. To make this more clear it moy be said that probably the members f teams in Liverpool, Wigan and Newton- le-Willows (forming what may be called the Western section). sill tourney to Warrington to play. It is whispered that the gam, will be played on the Cemetery green, which is noted as being one of the best greens in Lin.shire. If the games are decided at Warrington, then the entry will be a very large one as all the members of the Works Bowling Amociation are entitled to take port.

The club lieu been in course of formation during the past two years, and the turf is now in splendid condition. It has surroundings of green tastefully laid out with trees, plants and climbs, and ornamented flower and rose borders. The aspc.,t I presented is most pleasant and attractive. div.head: TO CURE NERVOUSNESS AND INDIGESTION.
div.p: TO CURE NERVOUSNESS AND INDIGESTION.
BY A MEDICAL MAN.

A famous specialist once said that nervouseess was the primary cause of nearly every chronic ailment. The work of all the vital organs such as the heart, stomach, liver and kidneys, is directly controlled by the nervous system. It is ooly natural then, that when the nervous system is out of order the work of all the vital organs suffer accordingly. Indigestion or stomach trouble does not cause nervousness or irritability, but, on the contrary, nervousness causes indigestion, which is the only way in which the stomach can toll you that the nerves controlling it are out of order. To cure this nerve illness, and at the same time the stomach, kidney or liver trouble, you get your chemist to put-up in an goz. bottle, half an ounce of Tincture Cardamom. Compound, 11. P., 2 ounce. Salrado Compound, and 3 ountes Elixir Simplex, and enough water to fill the bottle. Take a tablespoonful of this nerve tonic about twenty minutes before meals, and if particularly weak and run down, two tablespoonfuls may be taken. Chew your food thoroughly and drink but little while eating. NOTE : This is one of a seriec of raluable articles on the rare of the health which will appear in these columns from time to time.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There is many a pleasant surprise in store for the patron of the music belle, aud we must confess to considerable surprise and gratification at the excel- lence of a " turn " which is not in the bill at the Palace this week, but which has greatly delighted every " Louse." Two young lady acrobats and con- tortionists appear as "deputies," and secure the bulk of the public appreciation by their aimblenesa, dexterity and suppleness of limb. Some of the feats performed are remarkable, and should help these aspiring damsels rapidiy along the road to fame. Some excellent operatic singing is provided by David and Marriott a lady and gentleman who are gifted with voices of admirab!e quality, and bearing every evidence of careful training. Their vat ions tuneful items are among the most popular contributions of the evening. The Violas make a return visit and as usual completely mystify the audience by a skilful display of thought- reading or some other more or less occult science. whatever their method this lady and gentleman ere entitled to high praise for cleverness and showman- ship, Professor Norton also adding to his accom- prishments a knowledge of sleight-of-hand metiers which is fully equal to the thought-reading mysteries, and baffles the audience to the some extent Brun and Hemsky capably fulfil the obligations of their description of comedy entertainers, the extrava- gant dancing of the gentleman being exceedingly funny. Tom Lea spins some original yarns, which find a hilarious response even in the most stoical, and Fred Karno's latest creation, the " Yap Yaps " fulfils all amicipations— which is not exactly extrava- gant praise. The sketch is elaborately mounted, but errs on the side of vulgarity, and would be improved with a little judicious censoring.

'lho t,uu:sorne and snaci.is Circus at Ma, het dire, which Trill he the crowning feature of Warrington's scheme of street improvement, has been brought an Mir ortant step nearer rt alizalion. The lira quadrat t is now complete and it is pos,ible to form some con- ception of the magnitude of the undertaking and to appreciate how vastly different the appearance of tire historic centre of Warrington will he when Market Gate in transformed into a Circus 160 ft. in dianwteo, with the four main 'erects, widened and modernised, radi ding from it. When the project was under con- sideration,the Street Improvement ar.d Lighting Com- mittee wisely decided to invite c, repetitive desi,,,s for the architectural treaunent of Market Gate, nub the object of ensuring harmony and dignity in the constroction of the new !millings. The Pans or our townsmen, Ife,•sra. It right, Garnett and Wright, were accepted on the advice if an eminent ..ant'lority (Professor Reilly, of L•nrion our! Rowute Professor of Architecture at the l'niversity o, iverpool) and anyone desiring to boil,' on the :Irene cc i:1 be required toconform to them. To Meters:Root, Cash Chemists, belongs the distinction of ii inn the first firm to erect new premises in accordance with theee designs, and the lofty,dignilied and well at pointed Otop which ham just been opened at the corner of Bridge-street and Sankey-t-trett has called forth unstinted praise from all who have any regard for the healthful in modern town life. When the other portions of the Circus have been carried out on uniform lints, Warrington people trill indeed hare cause to be proud of the foresight and enterprise which prompted the planning of the busy centre of the town 03 these imp:sing lines,

_ In dean-rung the Circus, the architects tell its that their object was to suggest the Georgian Renaissance and, while making every proviaion for modern methods and requirement., to recall the period during which Warrington became possessed of the majority of the buildings of which she is to-day most proud. Holy Trinily Church, the Town Hall, the Old Academy, Garesbury Hall, and many other places in and near the town seem by their quiet and dignified appearance to faithfully expressive of the aims and aspirations of their builders and inhal,itants that one is at once reminded of many of the great names and noble characters inseparably ',rued up with the tradi- tions of Warrington. It was therefore (the architects state) considered imperative that the impression afforded by Market Gate should be characteristi,l of the town at im best. A stliking feature of thedeaign is the

tr.e of crni tasting rnatertal4 in large ma-se., affording a bright and cheerful colour act eme. while the minor variations of detail will materially indicate the diviar .n and extent of 'hops and relieve the monotony withr at breakieg the main lines. The Hauliers with carved hanging gatlands give a feeling of strength to the angles ;Ind cornets, while the two return ends, treated in stone tide-410, ut, form effective and convincing finisher, and lend themselvte, if neces-ary, as entrances to offices and chamhers on the nipper flows. lhere is no at.emyt to include a scheme for the provision of a central island or any architect- anal Seam.° of that kind.

Prof ssor Reilly in his adjudication laid stress on the fart that Warrington is iarticularly strong in good specimens of early Georgian r 181.11 century architecture which corresoor.ded t • the beat period of its Li+ tory. Such architecture Is more suited to modern needs than that of any earlier period and consequently forms the best starting point for modern developmr.nts ; indeed the finest currer.t architecture is a distinct continuation of the ideas which underlie it. In congratulating the Corporation on the choice of the Circus form for the junction of their streets, instead of the usual" troll-noon" endings, Protease, Reilly p into out that the former allow. of proper architectural treatment of the whole, which the latter precludes. It is a special honour to Warrington to know that the Cr cue will be the first of any magnitude which has been built in England since the beginning of the last centu7. " The form, however," adds the professor, ' is a peculiarly English one, and was used with great effect in the eighteenth century- the best period of English civil architecture - in stick cities as London, I.L.th and Buxton where architectural amenities were considered and valued."

The next stage of the scheme is the widening of Buttermarket-strvet which will very shortly be placed in hand—in fact all preparations have been made for the demolition of property. A considerable time will necetuutrily elapse before Sankey-street i tackled but the marked improvement already achieved is sufficient rto entitle the Council to the enthusiastic support of the ratepayers in their endeavour to see the complete undertaking through nith all possible expdition. The Circus will undoubtedly give to the town a distinction which many provincial boroughs might envy and the long rheritibed vision of a "beautiful Warrington" will approach touch nearer the region of actuality.

We have a shop which for size and style of finish would be an attraction in any of the most prominent West End Streets of London. And as we outshine in style and finish of our premises, so we outshine in the quality and low prices of our goods. Not only are we Chemists and Druggists having over 450 branches, embracing all the principal towns between Glasgow and the Channel Islands, but we are also the greatest buyers of Fancy and Leather Goods, Toilet Articles, Pictures, and Picture Frames in the Country. We extend to all a cordial invitation to call and look round our showrooms. There will be no pressure to buy.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SAFI:MOAT. MAY 13 1911.
A chorus of acclama- A GREAT tion from all parties has SCHEME. greeted Mr. LLOYD

GEORGE'S Insurance Scheme. The CHANCELLOR, reappearing after his long indisposition, signalled his return to the political field by making a great speech unfolding a plan of social reform perhaps more far-reaching in its scope and beneficent in its effect than anything this generation has seen. He puts before the House a stupendous project for insuring over four- teen million people against sickness, and millions more against unemployment. With infinite labour and great lucidity he unravelled the complex threads of this project, with its supplementary schemes. His tone was pronouncedly non-parti- san and non-personal. The man, for the nonce, was forgetting party and for- getting personality; his whole thought was for the work he was doing, his whole desire was to secure the cordial co-operation of all sections of politicians in the task of scrutinis- and perfecting the details of his bill. The House warmly responded to his appeal. For the Unionists Mr. ATJSTEN CHAMBERLAIN, for the Labour Party Mr. RAMSAY MAC- DONALD, for the Nationalists Mr. JOHN REDMOND, all heartily responded to his appeal, and generously congratulated him on the courage with which he had set his hand to a herculean task. No great measure ever started its Parliamentary career under more favourable auspices or with a weightier and more resolute backing.

The bill, the text of which has appeared, is of vast size and comprehensive. It would be impossible to set down here in all their ramifications its various clauses and schedules. But, briefly, its provisions are these. Every employed wage-earner getting less than £l6O a-year is to be compulsorily insured against sickness and invalidity whilst other persons will be able to take, advantage of the scheme in a voluntary I way. tinder the compulsory arrangement the workman will pay 4d. a-week into the State Insurance fund,the employer 3d. a week and the State 2d. a-week—women paying ld. weekly less than men, their benefits being proportionately reduced. The benefits will include a sickness allowance of 10s. a week for three months and Is. a week for another three ,months, with a permanent disability allowance of ss. a week. In addition to this, free medical relief and free drugs will be allowed—an enormous boon to poor people. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE does not stop at this broad, simple plan. He goes on to make an allowance of 30s. for maternity cases, provided the mother does not go to work for four weeks, and he sets aside a capital sum of £1,500,000 for building consumption sanatoria. Over and above this he is going to have a balance of lh million (which will be quadrupled after fifteen and a-half years), which he intends to spend on convalescent homes, on the augmentation of Old-Age Pensions, and other objects. The unemployment section of th

scheme is at present more experimental than the other. Two and a-half million men in two great trades—building and engineering —are to be secured an out-of-work benefit Of 7s. for fifteen weeks by paying 21d. weekly into a tund into which the employer pays another 2d., and the State adds one- fourth of the total cost. The total coat of both schemes will be in the first year no less than £24,500,000, the State's expenditure beginning at £2,500,000 and soon doubling. As all agree, the bill marks a great stage in the war against sickness and unemploy- ment, the most fruitful mothers of destitu- tion, pauperism and misery. There will cer- tainly be exhaustive criticism of the clauses relating to the relative contributions of man, master and State. The Labour men are con- tending that the whole of the premiums are too high in relation to the benefits, and many employers are saying, with some show of justice, that the contributions they are called upon to pay are too high and that the general taxpayer is let off too lightly. Every lesser provision also will be closely examined. Some, in our view, need amending. For instance, the maternity allowance of 308. on the stipu- lation that the mother does not go to her work for a month seems too low. Why not give the mother the ordinary sickness allow- ance for that period as well as the maternity allowance ? Otherwise, we shall not abolish the dilemma in which too many mothers are at present when they have to choose between rest and semi-starvation on the one hand and work, neglect of their new-born babies, and injury to their own health on the other. These matters will all be threshed out by the experts in the House. For the ordinary man outside it is enough to be grateful that all parties, especially at a time of fierce political conflict, should unite to carry through a regenerating scheme of this nature, and to look forward to a time when, owing to this and other social legislation, the condition of our people will have been transformed.
Mr. A. H. Croefield is MR. CROSFIELD'S again giving an inepir- POLITICAL LEAD. ing lead to the pro-..

giessive forces -of Warrington and the response is proving in every way worthy of the greatness of the causes which he expounds with so much sincerity and force. These are encouraging and heartening days for Liberals, for Mr. Lloyd George's great insur- ance scheme has afforded one more proof that the Government is not content with any mere hp-service to social reform but is always doing something practical for the benefit of the workers. In a very happy and appropriate speech at the distribution of bowling prizes at the Liberal Club, Mr. Crosfield naturally dwelt with satisfaction upon this beneficent constructive measure and also put in a strong plea for a clearer understanding on the question of self- government for Ireland, of which he has long been a convinced and fearless supporter. The Progressive Labour League's meeting at Bridge Foot on Tuesday evening found Mr. Croefield in his best speaking form and he held the close attention of a large audience for over half-an-hour by a particularly striking address on some of the pressing questions of the day. His warning against the double millstone of Protection and conscrip- tion, which it is sought to fasten round the necks of our workingclasses, was pointed and opportune, and indicates that gradual but sure stiffening of Mr. Crosfield's attitude .n the question of militarism which many of his supporters have observed with satisfaction for some time past.

It is no wonder that THE DEATH-BLOW. the House of Lords was frigid, and Lord Lansdowne himself lugubrious, at the intro- duction of the " Reform " Bill on Monday. As an alternative to the Parliament Bill, even Lord Lansdowne himself could not seriously regard his measure. The country is determined—and no " tinkering " at an old and decrepit House will turn it aside—that the House of Commons shall have the last word to say in the legislation which the electorate have elected it to carryout. Lord Lansdowne has so framed his Bill that the present House of Commons would find itself overridden by a majority in his" reformed" House of Lords. That may be a sop to the " backwoodsmen " ; even if he had framed his Bill with a frank recognition of the principle of fair play it would still have been futile as an alternative to the Parliament Bill. There is no alternative.

div.head: CHAPTER OF HISTORY.
div.p: A CHAPTER OF HISTORY.

..... IA fa Mum, Of Lord] stands impregnable, not merely upon its historic pest, but upon lu present utility—Mr. BALFOUR, October 22,1906. This Bill would beyond doubt be a deatb-blow to the House of Lords as many of us have known It for as long—Loan LANaDOWNR, Mayo lull. The two passages quoted above give us the beginning and end of a chapter of English history which must always appeal even to the most sluggish imagination. Five years ago the House of Lords did indeed, as Mr. Balfour said, rook impregnable. It had been threatened many times, but as many times it had defied its assailants and re-established its position. After the great triumph of 1906 it continued, as before, to deliver blow upon blow to the strongest Liberal Government of our time, and until two years ago that Government could find no effective means of resenting its action. Then suddeidy it did the one thing too much, and now its own leader comes forward, in his own words, to administer " its death-blow."— Westminster Gazette.
Mr Asquith' great MR ASQUITH'S speech at Manchester MANCHESTER was one of those close- SPEECH, packed trains of argu-

ment for which he' is famous that are the despair of the summariser. Instead of a summary, there- fore, it seems advisable to fix on two points which perhaps deserve the greatest emphasis. First, Mr. Asquith proved from the speeches of Tory leaders that, at the last General Election, the avowed intention of the Govern- ment was to introduce a Home Rule Bill if the electorate returned them to office. Secondly, the Government's epoch-making departures in social reform completely upset the con „ention of the Opposition that the Liberal Party is too busy " tinkering " the constitution to find time for social reforms.

It is stated that Queen Alexandra will not be in London for any of the Coronation festivities, but will go away on or about Saturday next to Sandringham or Windsor, probably the former. _

• • Among the many interesting topics dis- cussed at the Conference of Liberal Women in Manchester was that of " married women teachers." There was a keen debate, but when the vote was taken the Conference was found to be in line with the prevailing conviction of educationists that the place for the married woman is in the home and not in the elementary school.

A White Paper, issued on Tuesday, on the trade, commerce, and people of the United Kingdom, shows that whereas the population has grown from 24,000,000 in 1831 to 45,000,000 last year, the death rate per 1,000 from the year 1871 has decreased from 21.5 to 13.9 last year. A matter for serious atten- tion is that referring to the birth rate per 1,000, which has since 1871 shown a steady decline from 33.8 to 24.7 last year. • •

Sir Gilbert Gr..ennll has announced his resignation of the Mastership of the Belvoir Hunt, the resignation to take effect at the end of next season. In March, 1908, Sir Gilbert made an exactly similar announce- ment, advancing as his reason, that "revolu- tionary measure" the Licensing Bill. As there is no special reason vouchsafed this time, perhaps the Belvair will get a new Master "at the enct_otnezt season."

• • "Instead of a step towards political annexation, reciprocity is a step away from annexation. . . . The political bonds which make one nation of our States are not the bonds that really hold us together. But for Free Trade between our States, and the unity of commercial interest—not "interests" created by government, but interests spontaneously generated and voluntarily maintained by freedom of trade—s(c4lsion would be a perennial question with us."— "The Public" (Chica_o).

There is every indication (says a lobby correspondent) that the Government intend to get the Sickness and Unemployment Insurance scheme passed through the two Houses of Parliament this Session. It is ' admitted that the Bill, although uncontro- versial in principle and to a large extent in detail, will, with its eighty-seven clauses and nine schedules, prove an undertaking of great magnitude to pilot through its Corn - mittee stage. Much depends on the minister in charge, and it is hoped that the Chan- cellor will himself pilot the Bill through the Committee stages.

•• • When the first shipment of frozen eggs arrived in London from Australia their extreme hardness astonishe3 the brokers, says the "Mark Lane Express." One man calling at a shipper's office was amazed to see him taking aim at the wall with an egg. " What the dickens are you at?" he said. But the broker let drive, the only result being a slight dint in the wall. The thing being explained, the man took a couple of the eggs, put them in his pocket, and left to startle his wife. Arriving home, he waited till the family was assembled for dinner, and then banged an egg at the new dado. But the smile quickly faded from his face. The egg had thawed! •

As an illustration- of' the justice of the taxation of unearned increments Mr. Cros- field on Tuesday took a very effective example from the neighbouring borough ofl Widnes. He said that the centre of the town belonged to a certain family, and was of such small value on the death of the first owner, that his two sons questioned whether it was worth while proving the will. To-day the property was worth £3,000,000, and the owners had never paid a penny in taxes. It hardly needs pointing out that the people of Widnes have created the value, and are entitled to some return in the shape of taxation whether the present-day owners consider it spoliation or robbery or anything else.

5.• I With the question of public health and ' infantile mortality so much to the fore just now, considerable interest should naturally be evinced in the co-operative effort between the Health Committee and the Guild of Help to establish "A mothers' and babies welcome" in Warrington. The idea is to open a room or building once a week where mothers can bring their babies to be regularly weighed, and where they can receive helpful knowledge and advice from competent teachers. A Ladies' Committee of the Guild of Help has already been formed to I carry out the scherne,which will probably be ready for its beneficent purpose in the course of a month or so. By the way, the writer of "Jottings by an Old Journalist " in another column makes some useful and illuminating comments on the loss of infant life, and the inefficient guarantee for a pure milk supply which the legislature of this country provides. • •

A correspondent raises some interesting points regarding the conviction on Tuesday of a Latchford woman for practising palmistry, or, in the words of the police charge, "using subtle craft . . . . to impose upon certain- of His Majesty's subjects." The defendant had been holding the usual seances in a room of her house and predicting the equally usual developments of real or pro- spective love affairs and marriages. There does not seem to he much harm in the " subte craft," and those of His Majesty's subjects who consulted the palmist probably did so out of ordinary human curiosty and the love of romance. The intention to deceive or impose upon" has to be proved, as was made clear by a question in Parliament on Tuesday, and we hardly think the guilt of Madame Eloise was fully brought home to her. She did no more than what the gypsies of Blackpool have been famed for years for doing, and what swagger mystery-mongers in the West End do quite openly for a wealthy clientele. The strong- est objection to the practice of palmistry in this way is, it seems to us, the conjuring of a shilling or a guinea from the pockets of the idly curioJa It is one of the lent estimable
of livelihoods, and leaves the way open for a good deal of charlatanry and unscrupulous invention.

The end of Court mourning net free a at ream of pretty fashions at Sunday's church parade in Hyde Park. For weeks past fashionable women have been pining to be released from the dolorous clothes which have been the law of their world for twelve months. Sunday brought them their first opportunity with the result that between twelve and one o'clock the park broke into profuse and vivid colours. The double stream of fashion moving slowly between the Mable Arch and Hyde Park Corner gleamed with gay tints of cerise, blue, scarlet and green ; and the brightest morning that Coronation year has yet given flooded the scene with dancing sunshine.

div.head: LIBERAL WOMEN IN CONFERENCE.
div.p: LIBERAL WOMEN IN CONFERENCE.

For the first time in the history of the Women's Liberal Federation—which dates back to the year Ito the annual Council meetings have this week been held out of the metropolis. This Federation is an important one, consisting an it does of 100,000 members We women of the .North --tame of whom have,g ne as delegates every year to London thought it only fair that the Federation should by this tiros Ice it, way ii paying on a return visit, and a special invitation won extended to them not year to hold their meeting this year in Manchester —2ll incitation which they accepted. Therefore, this week has aeea the envir ,na of the Midland Hall streaming with delegates—from nine hundred to a thousand of them—frors the extreme North to the South of England, including Wale*, and the counties in between. The Warring- ton contingent numbered shoot a dozen including three officials. When the business began at 10 a.m. on Tuesday the hall was full, upstairs and down, and I the platform—being gay will. bouquet., presented to the chairman—was a picture in subdued tones of lcolour suggested by the half-mourning London " toilette, ' worn by the officials and executive com- mittee, presumably out of respect and sympathy for Lady Carlisle 111 her recent bereavement.
(ilay I say here, in parentliesis, that the dresses were as narrow as intstl?leyor.freedom of movement) " .

In the absence a Lady Carlisle, who has been the President ever since the Federation was formed, the chair was taken by Mrs. Eva McLaren, the treasurer, who in her address spoke with 'peat earnestness and feeling A vote of condolence with Lady Catlide was proposed by the Chairman, seconded by Lady McLaren. in a touching speech, and passed in silence by the whole audience atanding. It is not my intention to comment on the debate.— there was • small army of reporters And other, pressed for that purpose, and they did full justice to the importance and intelligence of what they heard— further than to say that they were characterixed by conspicuous earnestness and ability. Of course all the burning questions of the day were debated upon, resolutions and amendments passed with a few excep- tions, and the otters and execut ire committee elected for next year. To the Warringt in delega.es it tram, a disappoint- ment to find that Mr, t. A. Ilowalth lid not receive eutlicient votes ti place her on that committee. On two occasions Miss Crosfield took part in the discussion, which made us feel that we were well represented. On Tuesday Miss Crosfield was the only speaker against a reeolution deploring the increase in military •,,d naval expenditure. She said the danger of a German attack upon ne wee a reality, and she stir rated "national" training as a safeguard. The resolution was carried without other dissent.

Naturally, we were anxious that one eiaitora. should be favourably impressed with Man,.liest.r. sad con- sidering that there wait continuous sunshine every day arid that the Midland Hall was unique for their accommodation aml convenience, we felt that cottottopolis was looking its best. At the chew of the Guifereace on Thursday thanks were cordially expressed to the Mancheaver committee for the, excellent arrangements and hospitality ; the gado, log dispersed to he various destinations, awl en ended the very socceesfuf annual meeting of the Women's Liberal Federation. div.head: DARESBURY
div.p: DARESBURY

All Saints Church, Daresburw, is one of the most beautiful village churches within easy access of Warrington, and it has also many interesting associa- tions. The peacefulness of ita situation strikes the town-dweller as ideal and on entering the church one is immediately impressed with the arhstic taste and extreme care which has been shown in its enrichment, the general effect being dignified and well-barmonised, There is some doubt as to how long n church has existed on the presentisite, but the date 1110 appeus on one of the stones or the tower and it in concluded that in all probability the church was built in that year. Little is known of its early history bat the church was evidently rehash in the troublous times irntnedi- ately preceding the Civil War, as a boundary wall bears the date 1028. A further restoration on a large scale took place in 1870, the wink being carried out by Menses. Swindell and Little, builders,of Manchester, uoder the direction of Messrs. Paley and Austin, architects, of Lancaster. A strikingly beautiful feature is the marble floor which was introduced in the chancel in 1902, the cost being borne by Mrs. Lucretia Elizabeth Jones. There is also a very hand- some reredos. It is interesting to not. that the Rev. Charles Doilgson, who was vicar of Daresbury in 1827, was the father of Lewis Carroll, the author of " Alice in Wonderland."

The ',regent vicar is the Bev. T. T. Lee-Jones who before entering upon parochial work had had a wide experience in the scholastic profession. His father was headmaster of the Grammar School at Tideawell. Derbyshite, and Mr. Ice-Jon, received his early tuition from him. He gained a acholarship at the Cathedral School, ftt cheater. and in 1878 became a scholar of University College, Orford, where he graduated in classical honours, proceeding to the degree of M.A. in 1885. He ,vas ordained deacon in 1883 and priest in 1884 by the Bishop if Sector and Man. After having been • private tutor at Oxford, Mr. Lee-Jones wae appointed headmaster of the Grammar School, Peel, Isle of Man, in 1883 and remained there uctil 1888. He was beau- muster of the Ormskirk Grammar School from 1888 to 1894 i, in which year he took up the headship of Guisborcugh Grammar School, Yi rks, where he stayed until 1005, when at the invitation of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart_ he came to Dares- bury. Mr. LetwJones is a cousin of the Rev. 1,. J. T. Harwell, vicar of Walton. By his geniality and the friendly interest which he taken in his pariehioners, and especially in the recreations of the young, Mr. Lee-Jones ban gained the confidence and esteem of all those amongst whom be labours. The church is making steady progress in all its branches, and the number of confirmation candidates and communicants bas shown a very gratifying increase of late years. The VC.ar has always actively identified himself with sport and athletics and whilst at school end college he captained the cricket and football clubs and was als coxswain of the college. brat at Oxford. Since coming to Haresbury he has been captain of the village cricket eleven and has proved his skill with hat and ball. Ile is also a keen golfer and has woo many prizes. St. Ann's Church. div.head: Free Church Sunday School Union.

Thongh the teachers of the various Free Church Sunday schools in the town may not have realieed the necessity of loin dig u federation, the advantage. to be derived from a union were apparent on Thursday evening when Mr. Arthur Black, of LiverpooLdelivered an address to a representative gathering of teachers assembled in the Got borne-street Baptist Church. In the course of a short address, the Cr, creams said that if they formed a union he wax convinced that the Free Churches would he a greater power for good than they lad been lathe past. Ile thought a union would be to the adventage of scholars and teachers alike. Speaking as the chairman of the Liverpool Sunday School Coat., Mr. Black said it was a very happy thing when teachers could be drawn together and combine their activities. By the Union the teachers of the various denominations were led to, realise the breadth of Christ's Church and the gospel and that the great Church of Christ was not cornpr:sed loony one denomi- nation. Through the Union they cauld make a broad survey of the whole field of young life with canvasees from time to time, and thus the Union would become an actual propaganda society. Regarding the religious teaching in the Sunday schools the speaker mid that the fact of opening a school and filling it with : acholars and teachers did not do good tulles& they were nurtim.d in the love and knowledge of Jeans Christ and the extent to which they could improve the aystern was enormous ; for through the Union they could obtain lecturers to instruct the teachers who would become oaten efficient, sad the children would consequently benefit. REHEARSAL OF THE IMPERIAL CHOIR. The final rehearsal for the opening concert of the Festival of Empire at the Crystal Palace, which is to be opened by the King and Queen, was held on Saturday list. The huge choir of voices picked from 45 choral societies in and around London numbered 4,500 and is the largest ever gathered together in the great transept of the Palace. These have been rehearsed, first by their own conductors, and liter, in bodies of 1,000, by Dr. Harriss. Not even at a Handel Festival has so remarkable a spectacle ever been seen. Tiers upon tiers of singer:, densely packed, filled every available inch of space in the huge orchestra. A specially interesting feature was the rehearsal of the fanfare of sixtecn Bach trumpets which is to proclaim the arrival of the King and Queen in the Royal Box.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, II P
THE GREAT INSURANCE SCHEME.

..... No proposal was ever made by Parliament which demanded from the wage-earners such full and careful attention as does the measure which was introduced hot Thursday by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It is magnificent in its conception, but the extent to which it will affect the interests of the working classes, and the organisations for self-help which they have built up, can only be understood by a very careful study of the proposals in all their aspects and details. It is very gratifying to find that the object which the scheme has in view, namely to help the working classes in their struggle with disease and poverty, has met with such unanimous approval. The support given to the proposal has been so general and so warm that the opposition has been silenced for the moment, but it would not be wise to assume that strong opposition will not develop during the discussion of the Bill from parties and interests which are affected by the proposals. The sickness insurance part of the Bill practically covers all the wage earners of the country. When the scheme is in operation every man and woman of the working classes will be assured of getting proper medical treatment and some measure of sustenance when sick, and should the infirmity become of a permanent character, there will be an allowance of Is. a week for life. It would he easy to criticise the details of the measure on the ground that they fall short of making full and adequate provision for sickness and maintenance, but we cannot expect to get a full and complete measure as a beginning. This scheme is not the final form which State help for the nick,infirm,and unemployed will take. The main thing to consider at the present time is whether the foundations upon which we are now building our first storey are so well and firmly laid that we can add other storeys as the need requires additions. It will be an achievement to set such a system as this going, and so far as one can judge at present there is nothing in the features of the scheme which will pre- vent amendment in those who want to see the State assuming a greater responsibility for the support of the sick and the unemployed than is now proposed.

div.head: • USING EXISTING -MACHINERY
div.p: • USING EXISTING -MACHINERY

There are obvious advantages in using existing machinery for the purpose of national insurance. This removes the possibility of arousing opposition from quarters which could wreck a scheme which was thought to be unfair to existing interests. There is a great economy in using the existing organisations and in taking advantage of their experience. Any scheme of State Insurance for Sickness and Unemployment which ignored the existence of the Friendly Societies and Trade Unions would never succeed in this country, where these institutions have planted their roots HO deeply. It was a very difficult task to devise plans by which the co-operation of these bodies could be secured, but it really does look as if the scheme now before the country will succeed in overcoming these difficulties. It is no mean achievement to have overcome the opposition of the friendly societies; for these societies have a strong inherited and traditional dislike of the State, and a sublime belief in the all-sufficiency of self-help to meet the misfortunes of life.

- The proposals, instead of injuring thel trade unions and the friendly societies, are likely to assist them. This has been the 1 case in Germany where a scheme of a very I similar character has been in operation for many years. There the trade unions con- sider it has been helpful to them. Certainly the trade union movement has gone ahead with remarkable progress simultaneously with the extension of the national insurance system. This does not imply that there are no features in the measure now before Parlia- ment which may not require careful watch- ing in the interests of trade unions and friendly societies. The Bill will require careful scrutiny with that object in view. SOME MINOR POINTS.

At the time of writing the Bill is not obtainable, and it will therefore be unwise to offer detailed criticism. A great many points have been left obscure by the state- ment of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, but with this reservation one may venture to mention one or two points which do offer room for criticism. The diffecentiation between men and women in the matter of benefits is objectionable, and in fact it is very unfair because the women are to receive a

benefit who Ii is, in proportion to the respec- tive contributions, much lower than the benefit given to the men. The payments by and on behalf of a woman amount to Bd. per week, those of a man to 9d., and while the man's benefit in cam) of sickness is 108. the woman is to receive only 7s. Gd., whereas the proper proportionate benefit for the woman would be about Bs. 11d. Then there is the question of what is to become of the contributions paid by the single women workers when they marry, as wives engaged in domestic work are not to be included in the scheme. These and a large number of other questions of great importance occur to one in examining the outline of the scheme as submitted by Mr. Lloyd George. THE WORKMEN'S PAYMENTS.

The rates of contribution are the most important feature of the Bill. It does seem on first consideration that the rates are high for the benefits to be given, and that the workman's proportion is unduly large. The contribution of the Stale is small, especially its contribution to the unemploy- ment fund. It is very doubtful if the great body of workmen will be able to pay the sums which they will be asked to contribute. Those who are insured for both sickness and unemployment will have to contribute 6W. a week, and this is a big drain on a working man who has a small wage and a large family. It is true that if he can manage to pay these contributions he will gain con- siderably on the transaction, for his 4d. a week for sickness and 21Ad. a week for unemployment will be supplemented (for his benefit) by sd. a week paid to the sickness fund by the employer and the State, dond about 4d. a week paid by them to the unem- ployment fund—also for the workman's benefit. But though the workman will gain considerably from the arrangement, it does not lessen the seriousness of taking awayjid. a week from the insufficient means which is the condition of a great part of the working , classes. It is all very well providing for the workers when they are sick, but prevention is better than cure, and we should first see that people have the means of living in a healthy condition, and that they have the means to provide themselves with a sufficiency of food and other necessaries. But notwithstanding these suggestions for the improvement of the Bill, it must be con- sidered a bold, courageous, and statesmanlike attempt to deal with two of the most serious problems of social life, sickness and unemployment. It may be that when one has had opportunity for examining the Bill in detail some of the objections which appear from a mere outline of the proposals will be removed. The unanimity of approval with which the general principals of the scheme have been received is encouraging. The workman's organisations should give to this Bill such careful thought and consideration as they have never before bestowed upon a legislative proposal. Their representations will carry great weight, for the Chancellor of the Exchequer must be anxious to have a thoroughly workable measure, and he knows full well that if that object is to be secured he will have to enlist the sympathy, and indeed the enthusiasm, of the groat body of the working classes.

The proposals in regard to unemployment , are limited at present to a few trades only, but, it is understood that there will be some provision by which other trades may come within the scheme if a majority of the men employed in the trade express a desire to do so. It is a pity that the unemployment part should be so restricted. Seeing that the State is going to supplement the fund to the extent of one-fourth of the cost, it is not fair that the men in other trades should be called upon to suppert the unemployed in the special favoured trades. The proposals to spend money on sanatoria and to make maternity grants are features which were unexpected but which are none the less welcome.

div.head: EXECUTION AT LIVERPOOL.

Crewe in to have a canal, linkleg up the" railway centre of Ragland " with the Treat and Mersey navi- gation, and giving it access to the sea. This Is the ambitious project of a nomber or Meal gentlemen. The present canal systems do not touch Crewe. The Shropshire Union from Ellesmere llort,on it• way to Wolverhampton and Birmingham, pusses about five miles to the west of Crewe, muting the old town of Nettle iv h. The North Staffordshire Canal, on its nay from the Merrey to the Trent, debonches at Rookery Bridge, which is only mute three or four milee from I 'rewe. It IS at this point the promoters vriab to couple up the present system and extend the weterway to Crewe. A survey ham been completed of the land, and the route in described as singularly free from engineering difficulties. Negotiation. bane been opened up with Isndownere,•ed no opposition has beta met with from any of them, though one or two have not, up to the present, sctually given their consent to the scheme. The levels of the country are stated to be so uniformly favoursble that it is not anticipated that men one lock will be necessary for the length of three and a half tulles, while the gathering-grounds for water at points along the proposed route can be piped to yield an abundant supply. The turf:linos of the canal will be In Henry street, t •rewe, close ton poptilooa neighbourhood, whore a basin, whareen, and dock will be constructed and warehouses and offices br,ilt, These will be M clone proximity to the North Stafford Railway Cow- -1 espy'. goods wharf, and contiguous to the London and North-Western main line to I.iverpool, Warrington and the North.

BY JOUN STRANGB WINTEIL
CHAPTER XXV.

Slandford joined the others in hunting through the adjoining streets, hut not a trace of Simeon was to be seen. This was ominous and perplexing. Lawson suggested that the detective might have gone by another route. Despondent and disheartened at his extra- ordinary absence, they walked back to their hotel almost in silence. Disappointment awaited them at the Ilotel St. James. for Simeon was not in the hall or the smoking room, nor had he been aeon by any of the son 'ants. Chinnery saw that, under existing air. curnstaneen, sleep wan out of the question for the night, and ordered a bottle of venue elic. quo! and some sandwiches. The pop of the cork, and the amber wine bubbling in the tall glasses caused • feeling of fellowship and of confidence, and thoughts were freely ex- changed. 131andford placed his cigar ease at the disposal of his companions and the four men were soon smoking comfortably.
"Did Simeon have the diamond necklace on him?" The queation was like • bomb- shell cant into their midst.

"By Jupiter !" "By Jove !" • "Damn !—yea, he had," said Lawson as- commonly flurried. "You don't think he's bolted," came from Chinnery. "Devil a bit. But the diamonds are worth a fortune, and hooligans are plentiful. Why, these blackguards would knock a man on the head for a few sous, but for such • prise as the necklace, they'd murder a dozen people," so spoke Blandford. "The trouble," said Lawson firmly, "is not about the necklace, but entirely about Simeon."

Parlotte's aolitary orb fairly rolled in Ito socket. He valued the necklace at £40,000, and his commercial spirit bestowed spontaneous admiration on the reckless indifference of them than to the value of the diamonds.
" The necklace is worth a great deal of money," he ventured. "Hot money cannot buy back a man's life," said Lawson, gravely..

" Simeon can take' care of himaelf. Mes- sieurs. no one better," laughed the diamond merchant, thrusting his arms into the top coat held by Blandford. Parlotte acknow- ledged the courtesy, and poured oil on the troubled waters by saying airily, while shak- ing hands as they stood at the top of tho stone steps of the hotel : " Some men are born to hunt. Many to run; Simeon is a hunter, not a bans. No fear, he is safe enough, I'll wager. Au re- voir," waving his glove !Toni vely. But he paused under the gateway into the Rue St. Honore, moodily thinking, "Maybe, maybe, he is at the bottom of the Seine. "

The hall clock chimed the hour of four, and Blandford proposed to his companions that they should go to bed until time for dejeuner at eleven o'clock. After • spell of sound sleep -fcr all were tired out--a bath, and • rub down, they left their sleeping quarters thoroughly refreshed and restored to their normal condition. In the vestibule they in- quired of the clerk in the office whether Mon- sieur Simeon had arrived. The clerk replied in the negative. Before breakfasting, they walked across the courtyard, looking an- xiously through the arched gateway into the Rue St. Honore. The question each asked of the other was, "Where is Fe?"

Finally the three men sat down to break- fast, by no mean. inclined to partake of the excellent meal which wan aerved to them, when a letter was brought to Lawson, bear- ing the London post mark. The address was in the writing of an illiterate person, and Lawson lured the soiled envelope over and over in his hand. "Who can it be from?-" he said.

"Cot the flap and see," suggested Chinnery In cool, everyday tones. "News of Simeon, perhaps," iisid Blond' ford hopefully. Lawson gave • low exclamation of surprise. "It is from Miss Morant," he said.
A clamour of voice. calling "Waiter, waiter," drowned lallandford'a and Chinnery's a9tonielied exclamat ionn.
'By Jove!
This is interesting...

"My Dearest,—l am writing th; in pencil, the wash from an excursion launch nearly capsized the canoe, and she is rising and fall- ing like a cork, near the bank. For some days a ronghish man has been fishing from a pont moored in the middle of the stream opposite to our lawn, for we are at Marlow again. Count Rodriguez and Miriam motored to Bushy, and dragged me with them. I Wan awfully indignant and could not say a word of farewell to you after we parted in Mon- sieur Simard's garden. Should you meet that gentleman in Paris, tell him hie big dog calla on me every morning. Hut, dear Michael, I am rambling from the subject— girls do, you know, when they are writing to someone nice. But there, I nm forgetting the man in the punt. To-day I was pretend- ing to read a novel, though really I wan thinking of von. The sereentA were at their mid-day ince), Miriam and 'Mrs. l'ridge busy in front of the I 1111 l se, and I was alone and enjoying the fact very much. The man in the punt unmoored, poling sig.zag fashion to wants the bank, and ran into the bushes be. hind. . . .

was extremely nervous at his stealthy movements, and when he spoke it was in a voice that just matched himself. I nearly upset the canoe in my fright. This is what the creature whispered hoarsely, 'Don't scream, missy—yew pretty bit of muslin, I wouldn't 'urt a 'air o' yer 'ead.' "I listened, but pretended to reed all the while. . _

I'm a pal of the Kidder, I means the Honourable Alec Blandford, and the cove yew is spoons on is going along o"ini to Parer.' Oh, Michael, if you had seen my blushes! I was so hot and uncomfortable but dared not move, for the Oxford boat was going down stream. The man said his name was Joe Niggins, a respectable householder in Blacken-street, Camden Town, who paid his taxes like a true-born Britain. Would I write you • letter? He put a packet contain- ing envelopes and paper over my shoulder. Now. Michael, what do you think of that? My scribble was nearly finished when I asked him, ' who will post and address the letter?' ''Me,' said he. ' Me and the cook at Mr. Lawson's chambers is courting, miss, and her master forwards letters to the hotel where the Honourable is along o' Mr. Lawson.' The creature become most impressive, 'Write this missy,' he said 'Leave Paree, come and have a jaw along o' J. N.—on the lay of them boots.' "Not understanding half he said, I spell the words an he pronounced them. I am not un- happy. Miriam has changed, she is kind and affectionate, but seems terribly anxious about something or other, but I have not an idea what. My dearest love, I must close my letter, A 1,.. "P,.—Mr. Niggins Is staying at the vil. lege. Fondest love." •• I must leave Paris," said 1.4115013. "Can you give use a railway guide. I've just twenty-five minutes in which to catch the ex- press for London." "Anything wrong at Marlow?" asked Blandford, wondering at the suddenness of this departure. " Weed, no. My news in rather satis- factory." answered Lawson briskly, as be closed the railway guide. " Eiggins "Niggles ! What on earth has that rascal been doing?" asked Blandford in surpri,e. "Taming over • new leaf. By the bye,
he clams your palship and has forwarded this letter." _ . .

Although they might not require the bass elef at lir.t, them might come, time when they would. Tenor trombone and bombardon players, who were only accustomed to brass hand movie, were hopelessly at a loss if called upon to play from the untransposed bass clef parts of an orchestral or military band arrangement. This was not only inconvenient to everyone concerned, but was aufffcient to prevent them taking professional or other engagements with an orchestra or military band, until such time as they had learned a fresh method of reading. It seemed absurd that in a brass hand the hem trombone should play from the bass clef, while the bombardons— sounding an octave lower—were written in the treble clef. The remedy lay principally with the music publishers, but they might also do something towards bringing about • more inuaiCianly state of affairs, by endeavouring to persuade their young musicians to learn both clefs, and so prepare themselves for any emergency which might arise. LATEST SPOONERISM. This is not of the " I've-a-half-wermeitfirdein-my- bosom " or" occupew-my-pie " order of Spoonerism, though there might be a certain appropriateness about the latter. I refer to Archdeacon Spooner's advice to Churchmen as to welcoming strangers at public worship. It reminded me of two or three incidents. I number among my acquaintanceu an old shoemaker who goes regularly to his parish church sad prides himself on lite knowledge if ecclesiastical law. itt the place is crowded on Sunday evenings, and visitors had often been kept standing in the porch until leisurely seat-holdere had sauntered to their respective pewe, my friend intro- duced the subject for discussion at the vestry meeting. Ile urged that thenceforth it should be an under• 'tangling that seats remaining unoccupied five minetes before the time for commencing service abould in considered available for the nccomtnialat bin of strangers. This, submitted as a formal motion, was promptly seconded by the Vicar's warden—to the great delight of the proposer, who had in mind the fact that that official's wife nun one id the principal offenders aimed at, The resolution wan adopted, and on the following Sunday night the humble cobbler took up • porsition in the porch and calmly and con- ' Woolly awaited developments. Precisely at ft 25 he entered the church and marched Imlilly into Mrs. Warden's teal empty pew. A few minutes later the lady arrived, accompanied by two others. She stood in the aisle as if suddenly tetrifird ; then she glared at the audacities repairer of footwear, who, however, gave no. sort of riga On iecovering her voice, the indignent lady raid to the intruder " We want our pew for our friends." The waggish cobbler simply drew out his watch and t renewed the dial for inspection. 'the holy therettpon actually went up to the vicar miii made a c mip'aint, and, what is more, the parson returned with her sort tritd to induce the old man to sit elftwhere. How- ever, like St. Paid, nom, of there thinga moved him. All he mid was" Treat all alike ; surely a resolution seconded by thin lady', Imaband and agreed to by the vestry too man, should be respected in her case so in ethers." The incident brought to my mind that of the pereou who, finding a stranger installed in church in similar eircumetances, wrote on the fly-leaf of bin l'rayer Book "My pew," and parsed it to the one whose presence he resented. The latter added in pencil "Very nice pew; what do you pay fur it?" and passed it back. "BAD TRADE." Last week's story under this heading is the Children's Corner recalled that of the vagrant who, charged with " wandering abroad without visible meane of sub- sistence and sleeping in a certain "Ac., Ac., pleaded that there was very little doing in his line of brininess just then, but that he intended to resume his employ- ment on the earliest opportunity. " And," said the presiding Magistrate," what do you do when you are in work ? " Well," replied the impudent fellow, " I'll not deceive your Worehip ; I smoke gleams for eclipses ! " DAYLIGHT SAVING. What the paper cited in last week's " Examiner " (vide note headed " The gift of sunlight "I had to say an to Mr. Willeten scheme might of course be amplified. The principle of the Daylight Ruing Bill has been adopted in a few Government Departments already. In some of those asso- ciated with the Board of Education, the officials now arrive an hour earlier each day and leave an hour earlier than formerly; and the system works no natiefactorily that it is likely to be extended. In various parts of the continent. of Europe and America, too, the scheme has been or is by nay ol Icing legalised. INFANTILE DEATH-RATE AND MILK. The references—gratifying on the whole —in the " Examiner's" lengthy report of last week's meeting of the Town Council, caused me to turn up my back numbers of " Pearson's Magazine," and to read again the first of a remarkable scrice of articles on press- ing probletne of the day. It was on "The waste of infant life," and the editor showed therein that about half of theconniderabl7 more than a hundred thousand ehildren who fail to attain the age of one year really die from preventable causes. After &scribing the subject an one of the most appalling an well as most interesting and important, affecting as it does the welfare of the whole nation, the writer proceeded to deny that the high rate of '' infant mortality "—that in to say, of the deaths of babies under one year of ago—combined with the low and falling birtbrate, means pod this : As a nation we are slipping down that precipice of degeneracy that brought destruction on the Empires of Greece and of Rome. Men were wanting, and for the want of men those empirre perished. Calling experts to his aid, the editor reviewed the chief cause, of the shocking mortality einioog babies and the remedies suggested, quoting eminent authoi ities.Aldennan William Browl. bent net forth his opinion thus ;—" The production of infantile sour-cry and rickets by bad milk and artificial fools, and transmitted parental disease, are account- able for a certain number of early &mite; hundreds of babies are smattered every year by mothers overlay- ing them in beil, especially on Saturday and Sunday nights, which, of course, points to drink ; underfed and over-woreed mothers give birth to weakly chil- dren. The predominant cause, however, is that the children are not suckled Cows milk suitable for children is absolutely out of the reach of the working climes snd the poor in large townn. The milk supplied by retailers in the poorer districts is elate, often robbed of create, and prevented from turning sour by preservatives which impair ite digeatibility. Liverpoore Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Hope) made this startling contributi '0 —" In the course of an inquiry into infautile mortality, 1,082 families in which the death of an infant had accurred, were taken consecutively. The total number of children born in these familial had been 1,571, but out of that number 2,220 had died practically all in infancy, representing 487 deaths out I I every 1,000, a waste of life nearly five limes as great as the standard. But the most remarkable genes of excessive mortality occurrent in twelve families, in which the large total of 117 infante had been born, and no lea+ than 98 had perielied in infancy. Theme extreme examples, it must be remembered, are occurring in familiar in which, no far as niunicipal sanitation ie concerned, therein very little to choose between them and many of the families who rear all, or nearly all their children." The food factor may here he said to be supreme. I am inclined to reckon Warrington among the exceptions in this respect ; but, as a rule, the problem of tofant mortality appears to resolve itself into the problem of securing pure milk. lam not now thinking of what sane members of our Borough Council insist on pronounc- ing " tubercularosis"; that involves other conaidera- tioes into which Ido not non propose to enter. The process of cow-milking as generally carried on in this country has been described as "a process of unaciontifio inoculation of a pore (or almost pure) medium nith unknown quantities of unspecified germs." It is :trotted that were a pure supply of dairy milk necurell for all the babies in the reentry, the first essential step for putting down infant mortality would have been taken. Here in in account of how it's done in Rochester, U.S A., where the municipality eupplies ouch milk At the milk station on the farm the milk is taken front clean, well-fed, tatted cattle into sterile cans, which are carried to the barn in sterile cheesecloth bags. Just before milking the cows' udders are washed A sterilised cheesecloth fly-cover is placed over the cow, the first portion of the milk being rejected. So soon as the cans are filled they are immediately covered by a layer of cheesecloth held in position by a rubber band. The cans of milk thus covered are immedi- ately taken from the barn into the laboratory, about two hundred yards away, where the milk is properly diluted, sweetened, and turned off into sterile nursing bottles. The bottles are corked with sterile rubber corks, placed in racks, covered with cracked ice, and immediately transferred to the city for use, Of the cloudiness of milk prepared in this way, forty-three daily samples are fOUOII to average not more than 14,000 bacteria per cultic centimetre, while the city milk for the slime period approximated 235,000 bacteria per cubic centimetre. I know there in another side to all this—marathon one, indeed. There is that of the producer and milk dealer ; moreover, I have not been at all favourably impreesed with the results of some such experiments in connection with one or two Lancashire muoicipalities of which I have knowledge. THE BRIDGE OF EIGHS.

No doubt many of my young readers will have heard someone speak of the Bridge of Sighs, and wondered to themselves what sort of a bridge it was and why it had such a funny name. Well, the real Bridge of Sighs is in Venice, and str2tches across the canal called the Rio Palazzo, and communicates between prisons on the east and the Doge's Palace on the west bank of the canal. It is la covered gallery, and the prisoners were led 'to execution from their cells across this gallery to the palace to hear sentence of death passed upon them, and then were con- ducted to the fatal spot where their exist- ence closed. "The Bridge of Sighs ! " Well may it have borne this name! Who can tell the variety of griefs and fear and bitter regrets that may ' have filled the hearts of those whose foot- steps trod that covered way ? Who can tell the remorse for past crimes, the remembrance of happy days to return no more, the sorrow for a broken-hearted wife or for children soon to be fatherless, of some cruel wrong inflicted in a fit of passion, the terror at the approach of a death for which the criminal was utterly unprepared ! Surely every step along the bridge would mark a spot where the tear had been shed or the sigh breathed or the burdened heart had felt a load of anguish pressing upon it. Well has that bridge been called "The Bridge of Sighs." I have not seen the famous Venetian bridge, but I have seen "The Bridge of Sighs" at Cambridge, so well known to the thou- sands of visitors to the University town as well as to the undergraduates. It crosses what Cambridge sarcastically calls " The Ditch," a backwater of the Cam, and it is named" The Bridge of Sighs" because it is an exact replica of the more famous bridge of that name in Venice. As one looks at it, it seems as though there were a church built all the length of the bridge, a church with beautiful windows and superb carving. But this is a delusion. The structure is merely a covered way which leads from St. John's College to what is known as "The Backs."

div.head: VERY FAMOUS FISH.
div.p: A VERY FAMOUS FISH.

In Yes Zealand lives the most famous fish of the world. This monster rf the deep is known as l'elorus Jack, and has the distinction of being pro- tected tire special Act of Parliament. Ithetiter this honour is due to the fact that he is the sole survivor of his species, or to the circumstance that he voluntarily acts ns a sortsf pilot for ships is not qu;te clear. Certain, howWer, it is that for twenty years and wore this huge fish has met all the steamers bound for Wellingttn. whether they arrived by day or by night. Ile usually takes ups position ahead of theta inn Pelorus Sound, as if with a perfect understanding as to their eestination. Thus he earned the sobriquet of the ''tilot fish " chile by some he was known as the Lone Fish of the French Pass.

Pclotus Jack, to employ Iti4 more general name, is one of the " sights" on the voyage to 'Wellington ; sometimes passengers had such little respect for him that they tried to " pot " him with their revolvers, but this sort of thing won stopped when the New Zealand Legislature laid it down that the fish must on no account he interfere I with. Ile is supposed to be the last of a race of marine monsters which flourished in French Pass half a century ago.
