div.head: R. J. PEAKE.
div.p: R. J. PEAKE.
Mr. Smith, M P, and the Shop Assistants

Sir,— A deputation of shop assistants recently waited on Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., to ascertain his views on the Shops' Bill. We were asked to regard the statements there mule as confidential, but a report in the Irene to the effect that Mr. Smith had speed to give our views his sympathetic consideration, has led to an amount of rnisunderstandiag on the question, and, the members of the deputati n think, constitutes a breach of the confidential nature of the meeting. That being so, we crave the opportunity of replying. For the information of shop assistants in Warrington or elsewhere, we admit that Mr. Smith did promise 0 give the points we raised his synivathetie considera- tion, end that is about all he did promise. Ile did not promise to support any amendment that will be moved in the interests of shop assistants ; be even would not promian to press It's own amendment to the Shope' Bill, which would include in the term shop assistant, anyone employed in or about a retail business. We are prepared to judge Mr. Smith by his vote and by his speeches on the Shops Bill, and we urge all shop assistants to do the same, and avoid jumping to the conclusion that Mr. Smith is out to 'enlist them in their agitation for shorter hours and better conditions of employment, until he proves by his words and his actions that such confidence is merited.—Yours etc., A. W. PEARSON, (Hon. Sec.)
4, Ash Grove, Lstchfurd, May 10, 1911. Prices and Prosperity (?) in the States.

Sir,— I should like to make a few remarks in answer to the statements made by a correspondent in your contemporary April 29th. According to the statement made by G. Graham Anderson, prosperity exists only in the State.. My experience is not quite so happy. I went to the States in 1906, arriving in Boston and wearing lodgings for which I had to pay 5 dollars weekly, without washing which coet me another 2.. weekly. I bad to pay 7d. to have a shirt washed, 4d. a lair of socks, pants or flannel vest 71.1. each, and so 01). Then I visited a barber and had a hair cut and allays, Is. sd. I also visited a fruit shop (not a first class one) and found apples cost 21/ cents a lb. I paid 5 cents. 21d. for two small ones. In England the same fruit can be bought for each. I had to buy a cap (the cheapest I could get) and had to pay 4s In England the same quality cost Is. Railway travelling is a luxury, I can assure you. eapecially when one is hungry. I had to travel from Bostrw to San Franci•co and consequently had to get food at the railway stations, my breakfast consisting of p-,rridge and milk, a plate of sliced oranges, a pot of tee, and bread and butter, 2s. Pd. For my dinner I received a basin of soup, a small steak (very small),chipced potatoes and pudding and a cap of coffee, 3s. 9d. When I reached San Francisco I tried my hardest to get work, but failed for a long time. I don't think I ever raw no many men cut of work in my life. In oc,olier am' November 1908, 15,15111 were registered as ut.employed. After roughing it for three weary nt, ntl:a, and. pacing 251 dollars a month for food ink, I made up my mind to I get back to dear old England and it cost me 1:20 to do it. But lam not at all anxious to renew my acquaintance with Protection. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and I I,ad loosed a half years experience. I prefer Free Trade England with all its faults.

The wages are correctly stated by Mr. Anderson but be does not put the other side. A c minus suit of clothes cost trim .£3 to £7, overcoats the same. Boots, from Ids. to Sos,; shirts and vests. Is. to 10, each. Owing to excessive house rent, 75 per cent. of the people live in restaurants. My expel ience was as n single man. What chance fort man with wife and family ? —Yours dc
A. BCCifiNAN, 7, Pi iestlerstreet, Warrington.

Sir,—Vidi Visi in Into letter of Saturday last issues father sarcastic and states that I have proved nothing. If he is so sore of this— why did he write and criticise my letter? Surely the public are capable of seeing as well as he. I did not say that the youths of Warrington after seeing "La Milo" would flock to the Art Galleries, but that the performance would remind them that such p!aces existed. Certainly I said that "La Milo " obtained a free advertisement, and if Vidi Viii is no certain that the performance is immoral why does he continue to give it prominence? Surely his cause would 110 better served by silence. . .

To caet insinuations and reflections on the character of Theatre Proprietors because they run their places for profit '' is too funny if it was not f,r the serious side' to to quote your correspondent. Alter making these assertions, to sign them " Vidi Viii " almost proves that he belongs to that class of individuals, who, after making rash statements, find that if they themselves were known, such statements might rebound with increased force upon their own shoulders.

It illustrates the life of the Hermit Crab who, to protect his own body from peril, cmfisc:ttes the shell of a mollusc, thrusts out his claws and snaps up all things to his taste without fear of retaliation. I If extremists were allowed to rule, all cycling and motoring on Sundays, all theatres, football, cricket, racing,and every other arnumment would be cancelled. But thanks to advanced thought the likelihood is, that the extremist will become extinct first. and to this clam I leave all areculative p Motion. They are of the " riAldeous overmuch " who prefer t i build churches before hospitals, to offer food for the soul while the hotly is left prostrate for the want of nourishrneat and medical attention.

Wordsworth had • knowledge of and repulsion for such people when he penned:— " A moralist perchance appemrs Led, Heaven knows line to this poor sot And he has nwither eyes nor eats : Himself, his world. and his own God." . . . _ . . .

Without fear or trepidation I declare that the theatres of to-day are in advance of the theatre, of the past ; and the perfnitnance of " La Milo " and Variety theatres generally, are far more suitable than the conjured. overdrawn, despondent inferno of Dante's creating, which the so-called intellectuals swallow with •vidity. To the working-class I recommend that they laugh land laugh often, that they avoid most or all emotional i and passion limps which are the miasma from which insanity and suicidal tendencies originate. - • .

Mr. Beaumont would do vrell to reflect that it is usually when people have no arguments that they hurl abusive but meaningless epithets at their opponents. These tactic. may throw dust in the eyes of the foolish and the igoorant, hot they deceive no intelligent being, and it is indeed a forlorn cause that hay to descend to these method,

Mr. Beaumont Sal. that -Town Councils have no right to pass Women'aSuff rage Resolutions Suffra- gists are not concerned an to whether a Town Council ought or ought not to do this thing, but they are very much concerned at to whether Town Conncils do, or do not do it. But surely in matters of great moment, a Town Council may suspend standing orders. The farther Town Councillors depart from their usual procedure, the more cogent must they believe the que.sti,on at 188110 to be. . . . .

So I am insulting my case by saying that the Anti- Suffrage canra•s is discredited ! I may be insulting a microscopic vortion of my sex, of whom I have long been ashamed, Ind am I not Aro insultinga certain proportion of the other sex The Anti-Suffrage canvass was conduct,d by both sexes. It is Adam- like to give women the discredit of it.

I challenged Mr. Beaumont to give the names of the districts in which the Anti-Suffrage canvasa was taken. In his reply, he mentions but one di.trict, which accounts for 21t; out of 35,579 Anti-Suffntgists. Is this the only place he can think of where the knti- Suffrage canvass is beyond criticism ? It is surprising t find that the sponsor for the Conciliation Bill of May sth is the M.P. for this particular district, and the importance Sit G. Kemp attaches to the mid canvass may be gathered from his spee3h in Parlia- ment. He says -"I thought it right to consult my constituents. I hare miens to believe that they are entirely with rte. (The italics are mine). I am encouraged in thinking so not only by the support of those who represent the same city as !myself. but by the fact that the city of Manchester passed a resolution last year by an overwhelming majority of more than four to one not only in favour of the Bill, but in favour of giving facilities for further procedure with the Bill.' It is noteworthy that the 69 unprincipled councils that have passed , Women's Suffrage resolutions number among them

The plants will now have become spleolidly Walt lished, and the question of applyiag an early mulching will arise in the minds of many growers. They will argue, and with some force of truth, that the application of short manure above the roota will keep the surface cool end provide food for the routs. On the other bend one can question whether either of Omen thingu is tiecersary at this stage, and the general opinion would probably be in favour of the latter view. The top should be kept quite open by hoeing or forking; but no covering should be spread for at least • fortnight I yet, bectuse the pleanant showers will bring food and imminent, while fresh, strength-giving air will follow the water down to the roots. l'hinne things will do more goad in building up the plants thao specially. conveyed food ; there should hr plenty in the groon, to last plants for some weeks to come.—" The Garden."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Workman " and "The Ring of Iron."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Workman " and "The Ring of Iron."

Two dramas front the pen of the late Frank Harvey, " The Workman " and "The Ring of Iron," have been presented at the lt,.yal Court Theatre this week by Meters Harvey and Woods' Company. The sudden advent of summer weather has depleted the attend- aloes, but there has been no lack of appreciation on the part of those who have witnessed the plays, which de& in different wats with the tame theme—the wrecking of homes, the temporary triumph of villainy, with the u,u•l " All's well that end, well.-

" The Ring of Iron " has the additional excitements of We in the Australian bush and the immuring of a perfectly sane heroine in a private asylum wheie physical f ,rce in the chief method of treatment. The leading parts have been capably taken by Mies Mary Lovett and Mr. Charles Lind Vivian, both of whom contrive to infuse a high degree of realism into their interpretations. Mr. Vivian was particularly convincing as Sir John Graham, alias Gentleman Jack, in " The Ring of Iron." The mount- ing of the play M excellent, and the band. under Mr. Ilorrthrr,yd's conductorship, eubmi!a a capital light musical programme. To-night The Workman " will be given. NEXT WEEK'S PRO(ifiAMME. Next week Wan.on Mill's pictureralue drama " Th Wrecker of Men " will be the attraction.

CHURCH PARADE IN HYDE PARK. The Court went out of mourning for King Edward on Sunday last, and from now until the Coronation there will be a succession of events, making this the busiest and most brilliant social season on record. Accommodation in London is already beginning to run short. Every hotel is full for the whole month of June. Nowhere was the cessation of mourning for the late King more noticeable than in Hyde Park on Sunday last. Church Parade was gay with colour and more crowded than it has been since lb* Summer of 1909.
